steps.body: The model lists multiples of 4 and 6 and finds 12 first. Any shared multiple works as a denominator, but the least one keeps the numbers smallest.
steps.narration: The model lists multiples of 4 and 6 and finds 12 first. Any shared multiple works as a denominator, but the least one keeps the numbers smallest.

widget.prompt: Rename 1/4 into the LEAST size it shares with sixths.
widget.successFeedback: 3/12 — twelfths is the least common denominator of fourths and sixths.
widget.lowFeedback: That build is SHORTER than 3/12 — either shade more pieces or make each piece larger until the lengths match.
widget.highFeedback: That build is LONGER than 3/12 — either shade fewer pieces or make each piece smaller until the lengths match.

commonFractions.feedback: A single twelfth is far short of a quarter — 12 ÷ 4 says how many twelfths one fourth holds.
4/12 is a third, not a fourth; check what 12 ÷ 4 gives.

predict.prompt: For 1/4 + 1/6, is 24 wrong as a denominator?
predict.reveal: 24 gives a correct answer; it just leaves bigger numbers and more simplifying at the end.

cml.actionGoal: Rename both fractions to the same piece size, then count the pieces for g5u lcd.
invariants: Fractions add and subtract only when their pieces are the same size: renaming scales both parts of a fraction and leaves its value untouched, which is what makes g5u lcd a counting problem once the denominators agree.
misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators across, scaling only one part of a fraction when renaming, or forgetting to trade a whole when the top fraction is too small to subtract from.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If only the numerators were made equal instead of the denominators, what would go wrong?

widget.prompt: For 1/4 + 1/6, both 24 and 12 are common denominators. Why prefer 12?

options.label: It is the least one, so the numbers stay smallest
options.feedback: Correct — any common multiple works, but the least keeps the arithmetic and the simplifying lightest.

options.label: 24 is not actually a common denominator
options.feedback: 24 is a genuine common multiple of 4 and 6; it is simply larger than it needs to be.

options.label: Because 12 is even
options.feedback: 24 is even too — being least is what matters, not parity.

options.label: Only the least common denominator gives a correct answer
options.feedback: Both give correct answers; 24 just needs more simplifying at the end.
